task.title: Readiness 1 · Select through sorting
task.prompt: For every customer who lives in the USA or Canada and signed up during 2024, return first_name, city and contact. contact is the customer's email, or the text none when the email is missing. Put the newest signup first.
hints: Three things are needed: a filter with two parts, a fallback for a missing value, and an order.
Keep the two countries together so the date test applies to both. BETWEEN includes both ends.
WHERE country IN ('USA', 'Canada') AND signup_date BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-12-31' ORDER BY signup_date DESC
task.starter: -- Write your SQL here. Save to check.
task.solution:
SELECT first_name, city, COALESCE(email, 'none') AS contact
FROM customers
WHERE country IN ('USA', 'Canada')
  AND signup_date BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-12-31'
ORDER BY signup_date DESC;

fixtures.declarations:
-- This case removes the email of one customer who signed up in 2024.
UPDATE customers SET email = NULL WHERE id = 14;

task.feedback: Check a customer from the USA who signed up in 2023, and a customer whose email is missing.

task.title: Readiness 2 · Aggregates through outer joins
task.prompt: For every department, including any that has no employees, return department (its name), staff (how many employees it has) and payroll (the total of their salaries, or 0 when it has none). Put the highest payroll first, and sort departments with the same payroll by department.
hints: Which table must keep all its rows, and what does a department with no employees look like after the join?
Count something that is NULL when nobody matched, and give the missing total a value.
LEFT JOIN employees ... count(e.id) AS staff, COALESCE(sum(e.salary), 0) AS payroll
task.starter: -- Write your SQL here. Save to check.
task.solution:
SELECT d.name AS department, count(e.id) AS staff, COALESCE(sum(e.salary), 0) AS payroll
FROM departments AS d
LEFT JOIN employees AS e ON e.department_id = d.id
GROUP BY d.name
ORDER BY payroll DESC, d.name;
task.feedback: Find the department with no employees in your result. It must be there, with a staff of 0 and a payroll of 0.

task.title: Readiness 3 · Subqueries through changing data
task.prompt: For every product that costs more than the average price of its own category, return name, price and band. band is high when the price is 500 or more, and standard otherwise. Leave out products with no category. Sort by name.
hints: The average to compare with is different for each product. What decides it?
A subquery that refers to the outer product's category_id gives that category's average.
WHERE p.price > (SELECT avg(x.price) FROM products AS x WHERE x.category_id = p.category_id)
task.starter: -- Write your SQL here. Save to check.
task.solution:
SELECT p.name, p.price,
       CASE WHEN p.price >= 500 THEN 'high' ELSE 'standard' END AS band
FROM products AS p
WHERE p.price > (SELECT avg(x.price) FROM products AS x WHERE x.category_id = p.category_id)
ORDER BY p.name;
task.feedback: Pick one category, work out its average price by hand, and check which of its products appear.

task.title: Readiness 4 · Tables through checks
task.prompt: Leave out cancelled orders. An order's total is the sum of quantity * unit_price over its items. For every customer who has at least one such order, return first_name, order_id and total of that customer's largest order. If a customer has two orders with the same largest total, return the one with the lower order id. Put the largest total first, and sort rows with the same total by first_name.
hints: Three steps: a total per order, a position for each order inside its customer, then the first of each.
Total the orders in one step. Number them per customer in the next, largest first. Filter in the main query.
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY total DESC, id) AS position, then WHERE position = 1
task.starter: -- Write your SQL here. Save to check.
task.solution:
WITH order_totals AS (
    SELECT o.id, o.customer_id, sum(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS total
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.id
    WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
    GROUP BY o.id, o.customer_id
),
numbered AS (
    SELECT id, customer_id, total,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY total DESC, id) AS position
    FROM order_totals
)
SELECT c.first_name, n.id AS order_id, n.total
FROM numbered AS n
JOIN customers AS c ON c.id = n.customer_id
WHERE n.position = 1
ORDER BY n.total DESC, c.first_name;
task.feedback: Pick one customer, total each of their orders that is not cancelled by hand, and check which one your result shows.

lessons.intro: A database keeps data in tables, and SQL is the language for asking questions about them. Every exercise in this course works the same way: you write a query, save the file, and read what comes back. This module covers that loop.

steps.title: Tables, rows and columns
steps.text: A table holds one kind of thing. The departments table has one row for each department and one column for each fact about it: id, name, location and budget. A query asks for data. SELECT name, location FROM departments; says which columns you want and which table they come from. The semicolon ends the statement. SQL keywords such as SELECT and FROM can be written in any case. This course writes them in capitals so they stand out from table and column names. When you save an exercise, your SQL runs on a fresh copy of the practice database, so nothing you do is kept between checks. The file schema.sql beside your answer lists every table and every row. This course uses PostgreSQL.

steps.title: Predict the shape of a result
steps.text: Read the query and predict how many columns and rows come back.

steps.title: Read the result table
steps.text: The first line of a result names the columns, in the order the query listed them. Each line after that is one row. The last line counts the rows. The query asked for two of the four columns, and the table has six departments, so the result is two columns wide and six rows long. The rows came back in the order they were stored. A query that does not ask for an order is not promised one, which a later module deals with.

steps.title: Predict an error

steps.title: Read the error
steps.text: Check the example. PostgreSQL reports error 42703: column "locaton" does not exist. The numbers after the file name are the line and the character where it found the problem. Nothing is returned when a statement has an error. The message often includes a hint with the name it thinks you meant. Start reading at the line it names.

lessons.intro: The SELECT list decides what each result row contains. It can hold columns, calculations and joined text, and every one of them can be given a clear name. This module also covers returning each distinct value once.

steps.title: Columns can be computed
steps.text: Each item in the SELECT list produces one column of the result, worked out separately for every row. An item can be a column, or an expression such as budget / 12. +, -, * and / work on numbers. ROUND(value, 2) rounds to two decimal places. The || operator joins pieces of text, and text you type yourself goes in single quotes, as in first_name || ' ' || last_name. AS gives a result column a name: budget / 12 AS monthly_budget. A computed column without a name is shown as ?column?, which tells a reader nothing, so always name them. AS changes only the result. The table is not changed.

steps.title: Each value once
steps.text: SELECT DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from the result. With one column, each value appears once. With several columns, DISTINCT looks at the whole row, so a row is dropped only when every column matches another row.

lessons.title: Keep the rows you want

outcomes.can: Keep rows with a comparison.
Combine tests and control which one is applied first.
Tell a text value from a column name.

lessons.intro: Most questions are about some of the rows, not all of them. WHERE keeps the rows that pass a test. This module covers comparisons, combining tests with AND and OR, and matching lists, ranges and patterns.

steps.title: Keep the rows that pass a test
steps.text: WHERE comes after FROM and holds a condition. A row is kept only when the condition is true for it. The comparison operators are = (equal), <> (not equal), <, <=, > and >=. Text values go in single quotes: country = 'USA'. Double quotes mean something else in SQL. They mark a name, such as a column, so "USA" would be read as a column called USA.

steps.title: Count the rows kept
steps.text: Department 3 is Sales. Predict how many rows come back.

steps.title: Follow the filter
steps.text: The employees table has 24 rows. The condition department_id = 3 is tested on each one, and four pass: Priya, Hannah, Ravi and Julia. The SELECT list then decides which of their columns are shown. A column used in WHERE does not have to be in the SELECT list.

steps.title: Combine tests
steps.text: AND keeps a row only when both sides are true. OR keeps it when at least one side is true. NOT flips a test. When a condition mixes them, AND is applied before OR, the way multiplication comes before addition. Use brackets to say what you mean. Three shorter forms are common. department_id IN (4, 5) is true when the value is any one in the list. price BETWEEN 50 AND 100 includes both ends. LIKE matches text against a pattern, where % stands for any run of characters, including none: last_name LIKE 'S%' matches names that start with S, and title LIKE '%Engineer%' matches titles that contain Engineer.

From department 4, only Tom and Laura pass the salary test. Kofi, on 88000, is left out. With brackets around the OR, the salary test would apply to both departments.

lessons.title: Handle missing values

outcomes.can: Find rows where a value is missing.
Predict what NULL does to a calculation and to a comparison.
Supply a fallback with COALESCE while keeping real values.
Use a fallback inside a calculation.

lessons.intro: Real data has gaps: a customer with no email, an employee with no bonus. SQL marks a missing value with NULL, and NULL behaves differently from every other value. This module covers finding it, what it does to comparisons and arithmetic, and how to supply a fallback.

steps.title: NULL means unknown
steps.text: NULL marks a value that is missing or unknown. It is not zero and it is not empty text. Because the value is unknown, a comparison with it is unknown too: email = NULL is never true, not even for a row whose email is NULL. WHERE keeps a row only when its condition is true, so such a row is dropped. To test for a missing value use IS NULL, and IS NOT NULL for the opposite.

steps.title: Compare with NULL
steps.text: Three customers have no email. Predict how many rows this query returns.

steps.title: Why nothing came back
steps.text: The result has 0 rows. For every row, email = NULL is unknown, and unknown is not true. The fix is WHERE email IS NULL, which returns the three customers. The same trap works in the other direction: a test such as email <> 'noah.kim@example.com' also drops the three rows with no email, because the comparison is unknown for them.

steps.title: NULL spreads through calculations
steps.text: Arithmetic with NULL gives NULL: an unknown bonus percentage makes an unknown bonus. COALESCE(a, b) returns a when it is not NULL and b when it is. COALESCE(bonus_pct, 0) reads as: the bonus percentage, or 0 when there is none. Use it when a missing value should count as something. A real 0 and real empty text are values, and COALESCE leaves them alone.

lessons.title: Sort and limit

outcomes.can: Sort by a column and take the first rows.
Sort by two columns with different directions.
Place missing values on purpose and break ties.

lessons.intro: A table has no built-in order. If the order of a result matters, the query has to ask for it. This module covers ORDER BY, taking the first rows with LIMIT, and where missing values land.

steps.title: Ask for an order
steps.text: ORDER BY comes after WHERE and names the column to sort by. The default direction is ascending: smallest first, A before Z, earliest date first. DESC reverses it. LIMIT 3 keeps only the first three rows, and it is applied after sorting, so ORDER BY price DESC LIMIT 3 means the three most expensive. Without ORDER BY the rows can come back in any order, and LIMIT then keeps an arbitrary three.

steps.title: Predict the first row
steps.text: Read the ORDER BY and LIMIT, then predict the first row.

steps.title: Sort, then cut
steps.text: All 24 products are sorted by price, highest first, and then the first three are kept. The Forge 16 Laptop at 1649.00 is the most expensive, so it comes first.

steps.title: More than one sort key
steps.text: ORDER BY can list several columns. Rows are sorted by the first one, and rows that tie on it are sorted by the next. Each column has its own direction: ORDER BY country, signup_date DESC sorts countries A to Z and, inside each country, newest signup first. When rows can tie, add another column to the ORDER BY so the order is fully decided.

steps.title: Sort by city, then name
steps.text: Seven customers live in the USA. Predict the first row.

steps.title: Where NULL lands
steps.text: PostgreSQL sorts NULL as if it were larger than every value. In ascending order NULLs come last. In descending order they come first, which is often a surprise. Say what you want with NULLS LAST or NULLS FIRST after the column, or filter the NULL rows out.

lessons.intro: So far every result row came from one table row. An aggregate function turns many rows into one value: a count, a total, an average. This module covers the five common ones and the difference between counting rows and counting values.

steps.title: Many rows, one value
steps.text: An aggregate function takes a whole column of values and returns one. count(*) counts rows. sum(stock) adds values up. avg(price) is the average, min and max are the smallest and largest. A query whose SELECT list holds only aggregates returns exactly one row. WHERE is applied first, so the aggregates see only the rows that passed it. count has three forms. count(*) counts rows. count(column) counts the rows where that column is not NULL. count(DISTINCT column) counts the different values.

steps.title: Two kinds of count

steps.title: Rows against values

steps.title: Aggregates skip NULL
steps.text: sum, avg, min and max ignore NULL values. For avg that changes the answer, because a skipped row does not count toward the number it divides by. avg(bonus_pct) is the average among employees who have a bonus. To count the others as 0, give them a value first: avg(COALESCE(bonus_pct, 0)).

steps.title: Zero rows still give one row

lessons.title: Summarize by group

outcomes.can: Produce one summary row per group.
Filter rows before grouping and groups after it.
Read the error from an aggregate in WHERE.
Group, filter the groups and sort by the summary.

lessons.intro: One total for the whole table is rarely enough. Reports want a total for each country, each department, each status. GROUP BY produces one summary row per group, and HAVING chooses which groups to keep.

steps.title: One row per group
steps.text: GROUP BY country sorts the rows into groups that share a country, then returns one row for each group. The SELECT list of a grouped query can hold two kinds of thing: the columns you grouped by, and aggregates. Each aggregate is worked out separately for every group. A plain column that is not in the GROUP BY is an error, for the same reason as in the last module: a group has many values of it.

steps.title: Count the groups
steps.text: Twenty customers live in nine countries. Predict how many rows come back.

steps.title: Follow the groups
steps.text: There is one row per country, so nine rows. count(*) is counted inside each group: 7 customers in the USA, 3 in Canada, and so on. ORDER BY runs last and can sort by an aggregate or by its alias. Here it puts the largest group first and breaks ties by country name.

steps.title: WHERE before, HAVING after
steps.text: A grouped query can filter at two points. WHERE filters rows before they are grouped, so it cannot use aggregates. HAVING filters the groups after the aggregates are worked out, so it can. The clauses are written in this order: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY.

steps.title: Keep the large groups
steps.text: Departments have 1, 11, 4, 3 and 4 employees, and one employee has no department. Predict which department_id values appear.

steps.title: Follow the HAVING
steps.text: The rows are grouped by department_id, and count(*) and the average salary are worked out for each group. HAVING then keeps the groups with at least four rows: departments 2, 3 and 5. The group of one employee with a NULL department_id exists too, and is dropped with the other small groups.

steps.title: Read the error

outcomes.can: Join two tables on the columns that link them.
Predict what an inner join does with a row that has no match.

Join three tables and filter the result.

lessons.intro: A database spreads its facts over several tables. An employee row holds the id of a department, not its name. A join puts rows from two tables side by side so one query can read both. This module covers the inner join and the keys that make it work.

steps.title: Keys link tables
steps.text: Every department has an id, its primary key. An employee row stores the id of its department in department_id, a foreign key. JOIN departments ON departments.id = employees.department_id pairs each employee row with the department row whose id matches. The result has the columns of both tables. Because both tables have a column called id and one called name, write the table in front: departments.name. An alias keeps that short. employees AS e lets you write e.first_name.

steps.title: Join and filter
steps.text: Sales and Marketing are in Chicago, with 4 and 3 employees. Predict how many rows come back.

steps.title: Follow one pair
steps.text: Hannah's row has department_id 3. The join finds the department with id 3, Sales, and puts the two rows together. WHERE can then test a column from either table, here the department's location. Seven employees work in a Chicago department. The department's name came from one table and the first name from the other.

steps.title: A row with no match
steps.text: There are 24 employees. One of them, Alex, has no department_id. Predict the count.

steps.title: An inner join keeps matches only
steps.text: The count is 23. A plain JOIN is an inner join: a row appears only when the ON condition is true for some row of the other table. Alex's department_id is NULL, which matches nothing, so Alex is left out without any warning. The next module shows how to keep such rows.

steps.text: Both tables have an id and a name. Read the example before checking.

steps.title: Read the error
steps.text: Check the example. Error 42702 says the column reference "id" is ambiguous. After the join there are two columns called id, and PostgreSQL will not pick one for you. Put the table name or its alias in front.

steps.title: More than two tables
steps.text: Joins chain. Each JOIN adds one table and has its own ON condition linking it to a table that is already there. An assignment row holds an employee_id and a project_id, so joining assignments to employees and then to projects turns two ids into a name and a project title.

lessons.title: Keep rows without a match

outcomes.can: Keep rows that have no match and read their NULL columns.
Find the rows that have no match.
Place a filter so that unmatched rows survive.

lessons.intro: An inner join drops every row that has no match. Often those rows are the ones you want: the employee with no department, the customer who has never ordered. A LEFT JOIN keeps them. This module covers it, and the question of where a filter belongs.

steps.title: Keep every row of the left table
steps.text: FROM employees AS e LEFT JOIN departments AS d keeps every employee. The table written before LEFT JOIN is the left table, and all its rows survive. When an employee has a matching department, the row looks like an inner join's row. When there is no match, the row still appears, and every column from the right table is NULL.

steps.title: A row with no match
steps.text: Alex has no department_id. Predict what the department column shows for Alex.

steps.title: Read the NULL
steps.text: Yusuf and Mila are paired with Engineering. Alex has no match, so the row is kept and d.name is NULL. That NULL does not come from a stored value. It is how a LEFT JOIN marks that nothing matched. COALESCE can turn it into readable text.

steps.title: Find the rows with no match
steps.text: The same NULL lets you search for unmatched rows. Join with LEFT JOIN, then keep the rows where a column from the right table IS NULL. Use a column that is never NULL in a real row, such as the primary key. Customers LEFT JOIN orders, where the order's id IS NULL, gives the customers who have no orders.

steps.title: Customers without orders
steps.text: Twenty customers exist, and seventeen of them have placed orders. Predict how many rows come back.

steps.title: ON or WHERE?
steps.text: With a LEFT JOIN it matters where a test on the right table is written. A test in the ON clause decides what counts as a match, and left rows with no match are still kept. A test in WHERE runs after the join, on the finished rows. An unmatched row has NULL in the right table's columns, so the test is not true for it and the row is removed. A WHERE test on the right table quietly turns a LEFT JOIN back into an inner join.

steps.title: The same test in two places

steps.title: Compare the two results

With the test in WHERE, the three NULL rows fail e.salary > 200000 and disappear, leaving 3 rows. Choose the form that matches the question: all departments with their top earners, or only the top earners.

lessons.title: Use a query inside a query

outcomes.can: Compare each row with a value computed by a subquery.
Test whether related rows exist.
Avoid the trap of NOT IN with a NULL in the list.

lessons.intro: Some questions need an answer before they can be asked: which products cost more than the average? The average has to be worked out first. A subquery is a query inside another query, and it supplies that first answer.

steps.title: A query inside a query
steps.text: A subquery is a SELECT in brackets, used where a value is expected. PostgreSQL runs it and uses its result. A subquery that returns one row with one column acts as a single value, so price > (SELECT avg(price) FROM products) compares each price with the average. This is the way to use an aggregate in a filter, which WHERE alone cannot do.

steps.title: Compare with the average
steps.text: The average product price is 269.67. The Office Chair costs 289.00 and the Soundbar 249.00. Predict the last row.

steps.title: Two steps in one statement
steps.text: The subquery runs first and gives one number, about 269.67. The outer query then keeps the products whose price is above it. Seven pass, and the cheapest of them, the Office Chair, is the last row. If prices change, the average is recomputed on every run, which a number typed into the query would not be.

steps.title: Lists and existence
steps.text: A subquery can also return a column of values for IN: id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders). EXISTS asks a different question. It is true when its subquery returns at least one row, whatever that row holds. The subquery usually refers to the outer row, as in WHERE o.customer_id = c.id, and is then checked once for each outer row. That is called a correlated subquery. Unlike a join, EXISTS never repeats the outer row: a customer with three cancelled orders still appears once.

steps.title: NOT IN and NULL
steps.text: NOT IN has a trap. If the list contains a NULL, the test is never true for any row. The reason is the one from the NULL module: id NOT IN (2, NULL) asks whether id differs from every item, and comparing with NULL is unknown. referred_by is NULL for many customers, so a NOT IN over that column returns nothing. NOT EXISTS does not have this problem, and is the safer way to ask for rows with no related row.

lessons.title: Build a query in steps

outcomes.can: Name a step with WITH and query its result.
Build one named step on another.
Say how long a named step lasts.
Count in one step and filter in the next.

lessons.intro: Long queries are easier to write and to read as a series of small steps. WITH gives a query a name, and the rest of the statement can use that name like a table. This module covers building a result one named step at a time.

steps.title: Give a query a name
steps.text: WITH order_totals AS ( ... ) runs the query in the brackets and calls its result order_totals. The main query after it reads from order_totals as if it were a table. Such a named query is called a common table expression, or CTE. It does nothing a subquery could not do, but it lets you write the steps in the order you think of them: first work out a total for each order, then pick the large ones. The value of an order is the sum of quantity * unit_price over its items.

steps.title: Filter a computed total
steps.text: The step adds up each order's items. The main query keeps totals above 5000. Predict the first row.

steps.title: Two steps, top to bottom
steps.text: The first step groups the 152 item rows into 60 orders and gives each a total. The main query filters and sorts that small result. The test total > 5000 is an ordinary WHERE here, because inside the main query total is just a column. Without the step, the same test would have to be a HAVING.

steps.title: Steps can build on steps
steps.text: A WITH clause can define several steps, separated by commas. A later step can read from an earlier one. The main query can use any of them and can join them to real tables. Give each step a name that says what one of its rows is.

steps.title: Follow a chain

steps.title: What each step holds

lessons.title: Compute new values

outcomes.can: Label rows with CASE and order its tests correctly.
Predict whole-number division and keep a fraction when one is wanted.
Take a part of a date and subtract two dates.
Read the error from text that cannot become a number.

lessons.intro: A result often needs values that are not stored anywhere: a label for a price range, a number of days between two dates, a ratio that keeps its fraction. This module covers CASE for choosing a value, converting between types, and working with dates.

steps.title: Choose a value with CASE
steps.text: CASE picks one value out of several. It is written CASE WHEN test THEN value WHEN test THEN value ELSE value END. The tests are tried from the top, and the first one that is true decides the result. Later tests are not looked at, so order matters: put the most specific test first. ELSE covers everything that matched no test. Without ELSE, such rows get NULL. A CASE is an expression, so it can sit in the SELECT list and be given a name with AS.

steps.title: Follow the tests in order
steps.text: The Standing Desk costs 549.00 and passes both tests. Predict its band.

steps.title: The first true test wins
steps.text: 549.00 is at least 500, so the first test is true and the band is premium. The second test, at least 100, is also true for it, but it is never reached. The Office Chair at 289.00 fails the first test and passes the second, so it is mid. If the two tests were written the other way round, everything from 100 up would be mid.

steps.title: Types and division
steps.text: Every value has a type, and the type decides what an operation does. Dividing one integer by another gives an integer, and the fraction is dropped: 7 / 2 is 3. If either side has a decimal point, the result keeps its fraction: 7 / 2.0 is 3.5. CAST(value AS type) converts a value, for example CAST(stock AS numeric) or CAST('42' AS integer). A conversion that makes no sense is an error.

steps.title: Divide two integers
steps.text: Predict the first two columns.

steps.title: Dates
steps.text: A timestamp such as 2025-01-02 17:16:00 holds a date and a time. CAST(ordered_at AS date) keeps the date and drops the time. EXTRACT(MONTH FROM ordered_at) returns one part of it as a number, and YEAR and DAY work the same way. Subtracting one date from another gives a whole number of days. Subtracting two timestamps gives an interval instead, such as 3 days 18:29:00, so cast to date first when you want days.

lessons.intro: Queries read data. Three other statements change it: INSERT adds rows, UPDATE changes them and DELETE removes them. The WHERE clause you already know decides which rows are touched, and getting it wrong changes the whole table. Every check here starts from a fresh copy of the database, so you can experiment freely.

steps.title: Add a row
steps.text: INSERT INTO departments (id, name, location, budget) VALUES (7, 'Research', 'Austin', 250000.00); adds one row. The first list names the columns and the second gives a value for each, in the same order. A column you leave out gets its default value, or NULL when it has none. A statement that changes data returns no rows. The result tells you how many rows it changed. Run a SELECT afterwards to see the new state.

steps.text: Check the example. Error 23505 says a duplicate key value violates a unique constraint, and the next line names the key: (id)=(3) already exists. The id is the table's primary key, so no two rows may share one. The table is unchanged. This kind of error comes from the data, not from the wording of the statement, so it has no line number.

steps.title: Change and remove rows
steps.text: UPDATE products SET price = price * 0.9 WHERE category_id = 12; changes the rows that pass the WHERE. SET can use the row's old values, as it does here. DELETE FROM reviews WHERE rating = 1; removes the rows that pass. In both, the WHERE is optional, and leaving it out applies the statement to every row of the table. Before running an UPDATE or DELETE, run a SELECT with the same WHERE and check that it returns exactly the rows you mean. Adding RETURNING and a column list to any of the three statements makes it return the rows it touched.

lessons.title: Design a table

outcomes.can: Create a table with types, a key and a default.
Predict which rows a constraint rejects.
Link a table to another with a foreign key.

lessons.intro: A table's definition decides what data it will accept. Types, keys and constraints written into the definition reject bad rows before they are stored, so no query has to work around them later. This module covers CREATE TABLE and the constraints that protect a table.

steps.title: Columns, types and a key
steps.text: CREATE TABLE names a table and lists its columns. Each column has a name and a type: integer for whole numbers, numeric(8, 2) for exact decimals with two places, text, boolean, date. After the type come the column's rules. PRIMARY KEY marks the column that identifies a row. Its values must be unique and cannot be NULL. NOT NULL means the column must always have a value. DEFAULT gives the value to use when an INSERT leaves the column out. UNIQUE forbids two rows with the same value.

steps.title: Leave a column out
steps.text: The INSERT gives no country. Predict what the row holds for it.

steps.title: Read the stored row
steps.text: The row was stored with country USA, the column's default. The rating was given as 4. A column with no default and no value would hold NULL, which is allowed only when the column is not NOT NULL.

steps.title: Rules about values
steps.text: CHECK attaches a test to the table. A row is accepted only when the test is not false. CHECK (rating BETWEEN 1 AND 5) rejects a rating of 9. A check that involves a NULL value is unknown, not false, so the row is accepted. Add NOT NULL when the column must be filled in.

steps.title: Break a CHECK
steps.text: The table allows ratings from 1 to 5. Read the example before checking.

steps.title: Read the error
steps.text: Check the example. Error 23514 says the new row violates a check constraint. The row is not stored. A constraint is a guarantee: every row that is in the table has passed it.

steps.title: Rules about other tables
steps.text: REFERENCES links a column to the key of another table. order_id integer REFERENCES orders (id) is a foreign key. It accepts only values that exist as an id in orders. It also protects the other side: an order cannot be deleted while a row still points at it.

lessons.title: Rank and compare rows

outcomes.can: Rank rows overall and inside a group.
Compare each row with a summary of its group, keeping every row.
Filter on a window result with a named step.

lessons.intro: GROUP BY summarizes rows by collapsing them. Sometimes you need the summary and the rows together: each employee beside their rank, or beside their department's average. A window function computes across related rows and keeps every row. This module covers ranking, partitions and filtering on a window result.

steps.title: A function with a window
steps.text: A window function is a function followed by OVER ( ... ). The brackets describe the rows it looks at, called its window. RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) gives each row its position when all rows are sorted by salary, highest first. Rows that tie share a rank, and the next rank is skipped. ROW_NUMBER() numbers the rows 1, 2, 3 with no ties. Adding PARTITION BY department_id splits the rows into one group per department and starts the ranking again inside each. Unlike GROUP BY, nothing is collapsed: every row stays and gains a column.

steps.title: Two ranks for one row
steps.text: Tom earns 175000 in department 4. Priya, in department 3, earns 210000. Predict Tom's overall and in_department.

steps.title: Read both columns
steps.text: Across the seven rows shown, only Priya earns more than Tom, so his overall rank is 2. Inside department 4 he earns the most, so in_department is 1. The two columns use the same function with different windows. The final ORDER BY sorts the result. It is separate from the ORDER BY inside OVER, which only decides the ranking.

steps.title: Aggregates as windows
steps.text: The aggregate functions work as window functions too. avg(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department_id) puts the department's average on every row of that department. That makes it possible to compare a row with its group in one query: the salary minus the department average.

steps.title: Rows that stay
steps.text: Department 5 has four employees. Predict how many rows this query returns.

steps.title: Every row keeps its place
steps.text: Four rows come back, one per employee. A GROUP BY would have returned one row for the department. Each row carries the same department_avg, 64375, and its own difference from it.

steps.title: Filter on a rank

steps.title: Read the error
steps.text: Check the example. Error 42703 says column "position" does not exist. Window functions are worked out after WHERE has run, so WHERE cannot see their results, and it cannot use a SELECT alias in any case. Put the window function in a WITH step. In the main query its result is an ordinary column, and WHERE position <= 3 works.

lessons.title: Check that a query is right

outcomes.can: Count related rows so that none gives 0.
Explain and repair a join that multiplies rows.
Test a total against a simpler query.

lessons.intro: A query can run without any error and still give a wrong answer. Nothing in the database will tell you. This module covers how to test a result: know what one row stands for, compare with a simpler query you trust, and watch for joins that count rows twice.

steps.title: Know what one row stands for
steps.text: Before trusting a number, say what each row of the joined result stands for. After customers LEFT JOIN orders, a row is one order of one customer, or one customer with no order at all. count(*) counts those rows, so a customer with no orders counts as 1. count(o.id) counts order ids, and skips the NULL of the unmatched row, so that customer correctly gets 0.

steps.title: Count orders for a customer with none
steps.text: Felix has never ordered. Predict what his orders and joined_rows columns show.

steps.title: Joins can multiply rows
steps.text: Joining one department to its eleven employees gives eleven rows. Joining those to the department's four projects gives 44 rows, one for every pair of an employee and a project. This is called fan-out. Any count or sum over the joined rows is then too large. count(DISTINCT e.id) repairs a count by counting each employee once. A sum cannot be repaired that way, so add things up in separate steps first and join the totals.

steps.title: Count through two joins
steps.text: Engineering has 11 employees and 4 projects. Predict its joined_rows.

steps.title: Read the three columns
steps.text: Engineering's joined_rows is 44, which is 11 times 4. staff and projects are right because each uses DISTINCT. Legal has no employees and no projects and still shows 1 joined row, the department itself with nothing matched. A count far above what you expect is the sign of fan-out.

steps.title: Test against something simpler
steps.text: The surest test is a second query that answers part of the question in the plainest way, such as a count of one table with one filter. If the two disagree, the complicated query is the suspect. Totals are the easiest thing to check this way: a total over more joins should never be larger than the same total over fewer.

steps.title: Two totals for the same thing
steps.text: Both statements claim to give the revenue of delivered orders. The second also joins the customers' reviews. Predict which total is right.

steps.title: Why the second total is wrong
steps.text: The first statement joins each item to its order and adds up 52608.83. The second joins the reviews of the order's customer as well. A customer with three reviews now has every item three times, so the items are added up again and again, and customers with no reviews vanish. The total more than doubles. The reviews had no part in the question and should not have been joined.
